catalog_quote: 113.3. Stress. It is necessary to recognise three phonemic degrees of stress. Syllables are strongly stressed /"/, stressed /'/, or unstressed (unmarked). A macrosegment contains ordinarily only one stressed syllable. A stressed or strongly stressed syllable can only be one which contains a vowel. An unstressed syllable need not contain a vowel. ... [§130] A macrosegment contains one or more syllables, at least one of which is stressed with a vowel as the peak. Unstressed syllables containing a vowel can occur in the macrosegment both before and after the stressed syllable. ... [§132.2] A macrosegment can end with a stressed or unstressed syllable. Usually not more than three unstressed syllables follow the stressed syllable. ... [§300] a macrosegment is considered as equivalent to a word. audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The record rests on Crawford 1966, the standard reference grammar of Cocopa (Berkeley diss., x+252 pp), which we hold; every quoted passage was found verbatim at the cited pages (28-29, 34, 45, 56). The classification 'morphological' (stress on the root syllable, prefixes and up to ~3 suffixal syllables unstressed) is exactly Crawford's analysis and is independently confirmed at family level by Langdon 1977 ('stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word'), downloaded now from USC's open SCOPIL archive, and echoed in Geary's 2024 WAIL slides. Glottolog lists only two descriptive works; the one we lack (Bendixen 1980, UCSD phonology diss.) is not openly available and would at most refine phonetic detail, not the classification. no reclassification or re-read needed; optionally add Langdon 1977:239 as a corroborating citation. downloaded files: (SCOP

sources.citation: Geary, Jonathan A. 2024?. Stress-based truncation of loanwords in the Yuman languages. Slides, WAIL 24 (Workshop on American Indigenous Languages), 24 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Yuman languages regularly stress the root of native words (Langdon 1977a). Because of the predominance of derivational prefixes, Yuman words tend to exhibit word-final stress'; Cocopa loans truncate post-stress vowels to restore final (root) stress (citing Crawford 1979:123-124). Secondary source; confirms root stress.
sources.locator: slide 5 ('Previous work on stress in Yuman'); slides 8-9, 17-20 (Cocopa loan data from Crawford 1979, 1989)

sources.quote: p. 239: 'All descriptions of Yuman languages agree that these are stress languages, and that stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word. ... Uninflected words tend to have stress on the last syllable in direct consequence of the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes.' p. 240: 'regardless of the complexity of the word, the stress remains fixed on the root.
